title: National Federation of Independent Business v. Department of Labor, OSHA (2022)
shortTitle: National Federation of Independent Business v. Department of Labor, OSHA (2022)
summary: OSHA's power over occupational hazards did not authorize an emergency standard requiring vaccination or testing for 84 million workers because COVID-19 is a hazard of daily life, not of the workplace.
notes:
Key line: "Although COVID-19 is a risk that occurs in many workplaces, it is not an occupational hazard in most." Per curiam opinion.

Citation: 595 U.S. 109 (2022).

sections.Parties: Applicants were the National Federation of Independent Business, other business associations and companies, and a group of states led by Ohio, all of which had petitioned for review of the OSHA standard and then asked the Supreme Court for emergency stays. Respondents were the Department of Labor and its Occupational Safety and Health Administration, along with the Secretary of Labor. Employers objected to the cost and disruption of enforcing vaccination or weekly testing. OSHA argued that the standard was necessary to protect employees from grave danger and fell within its authority to regulate workplace hazards.
sections.Material Facts: On September 9, 2021, President Biden announced a plan to require employers with at least 100 employees to ensure their workers were vaccinated or tested weekly. On November 5, 2021, OSHA issued an emergency temporary standard under 29 U.S.C. 655(c), which permits standards to take effect without notice and comment when employees face grave danger from toxic substances, harmful agents or new hazards and the standard is necessary. The rule covered about 84 million workers at employers with 100 or more employees, required vaccination or weekly testing at the worker's own expense plus masking, preempted contrary state laws, and exempted only workers who worked fully remotely or exclusively outdoors. OSHA had used its emergency power nine times before, and only one such rule had been fully upheld in court.
sections.Procedural History: Petitions for review were filed in every regional court of appeals. The Fifth Circuit stayed the standard on November 12, 2021. The cases were consolidated by lottery in the Sixth Circuit, which dissolved the stay on December 17, 2021, and allowed the rule to take effect. The challengers applied to the Supreme Court for stays. The Court heard argument on January 7, 2022, and on January 13, 2022 granted the applications and stayed the standard pending disposition of the petitions in the Sixth Circuit and any certiorari proceedings.
sections.Issue: The Occupational Safety and Health Act allows OSHA to issue an emergency temporary standard without notice and comment when employees are exposed to grave danger from toxic substances, harmful agents or new hazards and the standard is necessary to protect them. OSHA invoked that power to require vaccination or weekly testing for about 84 million workers. Were the applicants likely to succeed in showing that the Act did not authorize this emergency standard, so that a stay of the rule pending review in the Sixth Circuit was warranted?
sections.Holding: Yes. The Act empowers OSHA to set workplace safety standards, not broad public health measures. COVID-19 is a universal risk that spreads at home, in schools and everywhere people gather, so the standard regulates the hazards of daily life rather than occupational hazards. A mandate of this breadth requires clear congressional authorization, which the Act does not supply. The stays were granted.
sections.Reasoning: The per curiam opinion described the mandate as a significant encroachment into the lives and health of a vast number of employees and said that the Court expects Congress to speak clearly when authorizing an agency to exercise powers of vast economic and political significance. The Act's text repeatedly refers to occupational safety, work-related dangers and the safety of employees. Although COVID-19 is present in many workplaces, it is not an occupational hazard in most, and treating it as one would permit OSHA to regulate crime, air pollution or any communicable disease simply because most Americans have jobs. OSHA's lack of any prior mandate of this kind, and Congress's failure to enact a similar measure despite extensive pandemic legislation, confirmed the reading. The Court distinguished targeted regulations that OSHA could still adopt, such as rules for researchers who work with the virus or for particularly crowded or cramped settings where the danger is workplace specific. Because the standard was not so tailored, the applicants were likely to prevail, and the equities favored a stay given the costs to employers and the many workers who would leave their jobs.

topics.lrs-i-major-questions: The note emphasizes novelty and breadth of the claimed occupational-safety power in an emergency review posture.
topics.lrs-s-delegation-dimensions: Gorsuch's concurrence frames the major questions doctrine as enforcing nondelegation limits on the scope of power an agency may claim, tying the case to the breadth-versus-specificity analysis.

learning.separateOpinions: The vote was 6 to 3. Justice Gorsuch concurred, joined by Justices Thomas and Alito, describing the major questions doctrine and the nondelegation principle as related safeguards of the separation of powers and emphasizing that states and Congress, not OSHA, hold the power to address a pandemic. Justices Breyer, Sotomayor and Kagan filed a joint dissent, arguing that the Act plainly covers new hazards and agents physically harmful to employees, that COVID-19 spreads in workplaces where people gather indoors for hours, and that the Court substituted its judgment for that of the expert agency.
